feedback: If the drawn blocks no longer match the cube counts, re-pair each block with one cube and recount.
If a learner cannot say what one block represents, return to the cubes and name the unit aloud before drawing.
activities.intendedInsight: The drawn block is a shorthand for an equal physical unit; moving from cubes to the drawn bar preserves the equal-unit meaning rather than inventing a new rule.
learnerActions: Lay out coloured cubes or counters for a part-to-part ratio — e.g. 1 cube of concentrate for every 4 cubes of water.
Count the total cubes and share a given total across them so each cube (block) gets an equal value.
Redraw the same arrangement as a labelled bar diagram, matching one block to one cube.
State in words what each block stands for before doing any arithmetic.
activities.title: Concrete first: build the ratio with cubes, then draw it

feedback: For a wrong match, ask which feature of the diagram (number of blocks, brace span) contradicts the chosen problem.
For an unequal-block choice, restate that every block must be the same size.
Note that selecting a correct answer here is recognition; follow it with a sketch so the learner constructs, not just identifies.
activities.intendedInsight: Interpreting and translating between words and bar models — and noticing where equal-unit or part/whole choices go wrong — shows command of the representation beyond surface recognition.
learnerActions: Match bar diagrams to the worded problems they represent.
Read a quantity off a labelled bar, watching for traps: a distractor assuming unequal blocks, and a distractor confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole.
Sketch the blocks for a given ratio (e.g. draw the layout for sharing a stated total in a stated ratio).
activities.title: Match, read and sketch (assessment-style practice)

feedback: If a learner always reaches for one tool, pose a problem where the other is clearly more efficient and ask them to justify the switch.
Verbal explanation checks reasoning; pair it with building or reading a model so the visual-spatial structure is also constructed, not only described.
activities.intendedInsight: Different representations often suit different questions — bar models are especially clear for sharing a fixed total, while tables and double number lines are often convenient for scaling a rate (though each can solve both) — and being able to choose and justify a representation shows flexible understanding.
learnerActions: Solve the same problem with a bar model and then with a ratio table or double number line.
For a fixed-total sharing problem and for a scaling-up-a-rate problem, decide which representation is most useful and say why.
Discuss with a mentor or partner: 'What does each block stand for? What is the total? Which tool fits this question best?'
activities.title: Compare the bar model with tables and double number lines
